walkthroughs.body_html:
HL Extension Topics and Quantitative Analysis — a core area of Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

HL Extension Topics and Quantitative Analysis brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with HL Extension Topics and Quantitative Analysis.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Alfred Marshall published 'Principles of Economics' establishing supply-demand analysis in:
A fall in the price of a substitute good causes demand to:
options: Decrease (curve shifts left)
Increase (shifts right)
Stay constant
Become vertical

mcqs.q: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier?
options: Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
The fiscal multiplier is always 2 or 3.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Mainly the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) — the higher the share of extra income people spend domestically, the bigger the multiplier. Leakages (saving, imports, taxes) reduce the multiplier.
The change from one additional unit — marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit; marginal utility is the satisfaction from one more unit. Marginal is incremental, not total or average.
Marginal cost is the total cost of producing all units.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Marginal means unimportant or small.

mcqs.q: What components make up aggregate demand?
options: Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
Aggregate demand is just the total amount consumers want to buy.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
AD = C + I + G + (X - M): consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. A shift in any component shifts the AD curve.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Consumer surplus”?
options: Alfred Marshall's demand-supply diagram in 'Principles of Economics' 1890.
Quantity producers willing and able to sell at each price; usually positively sloped.
Area below demand curve above price; willingness to pay minus actual price.
Price change moves along curve; non-price determinants shift curve entirely.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Equilibrium”?
options: Price change moves along curve; non-price determinants shift curve entirely.
Alfred Marshall's demand-supply diagram in 'Principles of Economics' 1890.
Quantity producers willing and able to sell at each price; usually positively sloped.
Price where Qd = Qs; market clears with no shortage or surplus.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Supply”?
options: Price change moves along curve; non-price determinants shift curve entirely.
Quantity producers willing and able to sell at each price; usually positively sloped.
Quantity of good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, ceteris paribus; inverse relation to price.
Price where Qd = Qs; market clears with no shortage or surplus.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Demand”?
options: Quantity of good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, ceteris paribus; inverse relation to price.
Area below demand curve above price; willingness to pay minus actual price.
Alfred Marshall's demand-supply diagram in 'Principles of Economics' 1890.
Price where Qd = Qs; market clears with no shortage or surplus.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Shifts vs movements”?
options: Quantity of good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, ceteris paribus; inverse relation to price.
Price change moves along curve; non-price determinants shift curve entirely.
Alfred Marshall's demand-supply diagram in 'Principles of Economics' 1890.
Area below demand curve above price; willingness to pay minus actual price.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Marshallian cross”?
options: Quantity producers willing and able to sell at each price; usually positively sloped.
Alfred Marshall's demand-supply diagram in 'Principles of Economics' 1890.
Price where Qd = Qs; market clears with no shortage or surplus.
Price change moves along curve; non-price determinants shift curve entirely.
